content_list.content_text: Asia has been making films since the silent era. Japan was retelling stories from kabuki theater as early as the beginning of the 20th century, while the first Indian film, Raja Harishchandra (1913), dates from 1913. Japanese cinema enjoyed its first golden age in the 1930s, with directors such as Kenji Mizoguchi (1898-1956), Yasujiro Ozu (1903-1963) and Hiroshi Shimizu (1903-1966), all making incredible films in an unmistakably Japanese style and idiom. In China, at the same time, films were being produced in the Shanghai film hub, where directors such as Yu Sun (1900-1990) opted for a realistic melodramatic style to examine the problems of the gigantic and fragile nation, beset by external threats and internal disunity.

information.contentText: Starring Toshirō Mifune, Machiko Kyō and Masayuki Mori, the film has an unconventional narrative structure that suggests the impossibility of getting at the truth about an event when there are conflicting points of view. In English as well as other languages, "Rashomon" has become a byword for any situation in which the truth of an event is hard to verify because of the conflicting accounts of different witnesses. In psychology, the film has lent its name to the so-called "Rashomon effect".

content_list.title: Akira Kurosawa - Composing Movement
content_list.description: Can movement tell a story? Of course, if you're as talented as Akira Kurosawa. More than any other filmmaker, he had an innate understanding of movement and how to capture it on screen. Join Taylor today in studying the master, possibly the greatest composer of movement in film history.

content_list.content_text: Until the 1950s, however, Asian cinema remained practically unknown in the West. A few Japanese films were shown in Europe and North America before World War II, as were some Indian silent films directed by the German Franz Osten (1876-1956). But it was the screening of Akira Kurosawa's (1910-1998) Rashomon (1950) at the 1951 Venice Film Festival, where it won the Golden Lion, that drew audiences around the world to the richness of Japanese cinema, starting a process that would lead to greater acclaim for Asian cinema in the West.

Kurosawa was a fitting ambassador for Japanese cinema. A liberal humanist, he dealt with seemingly universal themes, exploring the inaccessibility of truth in Rashomon and depicting a man's response to mortality in Ikiru (1952). An admirer of Western culture, he adapted the literature of his favorite authors for the screen, transplanting Dostoevsky to Hokkaido in Hakuchi (The Idiot, 1951) and blending Japanese and Jacobean theatrical traditions in his samurai Macbeth, Kumonosu Jo (Throne of Blood, 1957).

quote.quote: It's human to lie. Most of the time we can't even be honest with ourselves.
quote.author: Commoner (Kichijiro Ueda) in Rashomon (1950)

content_list.content_text: Given this Western influence, it is no surprise that his work received so much acclaim abroad, nor that his admired samurai films, Shichinin no Samurai (Seven Samurai, 1954) and Yojimbo (1961), were remade as Westerns.

Kurosawa's triumph in Venice helped draw the world's attention to other Japanese directors, many of whom had been making films since the silent era. The serene films from the final phase of Kenji Mizoguchi's (1898-1956) career, particularly Saikaku Ichidai Onna (The Life of Oharu, 1952), Ugetsu monogatari (Ugetsu, 1953) and Sanshô Dayû (Sansho the Bailiff, 1954), combine a profound humanism with extraordinary aesthetic beauty.

information.contentTitle: Trailer do filme Os sete samurais (1954)
information.contentText: Seven Samurai was a technical and creative watershed that became the highest-grossing film in Japan and set a new standard for the industry. It has remained highly influential, often regarded as one of the most "remade, reworked and referenced" films in cinema. The film's look, plot and dialogue have inspired a wide range of filmmakers, from George Lucas to Quentin Tarantino.

content_list.content_text: Mizoguchi's use of the moving camera is unrivaled in delicacy and precision, but his style was never merely decorative. On the contrary, it always served to visually express the emotions and circumstances of his characters. By contrast, another master of postwar Japanese cinema, Yasujiro Ozu (1903-1963), rarely moved the camera, opting for a quieter, more austere style for telling his subtle stories of the Japanese family. In films such as Banshun (Late Spring, 1949), Bakushu (Early Summer, 1951) and Tôkyô monogatari (Tokyo Story, 1953), Ozu explores the troubled relationships between parents and children with compassion and a resigned wisdom.

content_list.title: The Japanese Revolution in Cinema
content_list.description:
Akira Kurosawa is the best-known Japanese director in the world. Seven Samurai, a thrilling and humane epic, is his most enduringly popular masterpiece and also his most watched film. The electrifying, if less profound, Hollywood remake The Magnificent Seven (1960) is the most successful of the many Westerns based on Kurosawa's work - including The Outrage (1964), a reworking of Rashomon (1950), and the seminal spaghetti Western Per un pugno di dollari (A Fistful of Dollars, 1964), which Sergio Leone (1929-1989) lifted wholesale from Yojimbo (1961).

This enjoyable cultural exchange is delightful proof of cinema's universal language and appeal. Kurosawa drew inspiration from John Ford's Westerns and made something that boldly breaks with the limited traditions of the typical Japanese jidaigeki - a period film emphasizing sword fights in a medieval Japan portrayed as a fantasy land. Seven Samurai is packed with astonishing action scenes, comic incidents, misadventures, social drama, great character development and the conflict between duty and desire, all handled with impeccable attention to realism.

The film is light, nimble and economical, doing away with unnecessary explanations. It evokes mystery and sustains a mood of apprehension - with brief shots and quick cuts making up the peasants' search for potential protectors and their pleading of their case to Kambei. There are many scenes of overwhelming visual and emotional power - a dying woman dragging herself out of a burning mill and handing her baby to Kikuchiyo, who sits in the stream in shock, sobbing and crying out: "This baby is me. The same thing happened to me", as the blazing mill wheel turns behind him. Yet the film's finest moment is its ending: the three survivors gaze at their comrades' graves while the peasants below, oblivious, turn all their attention to the joyful ritual of planting rice.
content_list.credits: Original review by Angela Errigo, adapted from the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

content_list.content_text: These great directors were just the best among many notable filmmakers working in the productive postwar Japanese film industry. They include Heinosuke Gosho (1902-1981), a subtle and versatile director whose films capture an intriguing mix of moods; Kon Ichikawa (1915-2008), a virulent social critic whose best films savagely satirize postwar society; Keisuke Kinoshita (1912-1998), director of subtle, sentimental melodramas, unusual in Japan; Mikio Naruse (1905-1969), director of moving stories of strong women going through hardship; Kozaburo Yoshimura (1911-2000), director of restrained dramas, also focused on female characters; and Masaki Kobayashi (1916-1996), the humanist director of the epic war trilogy The Human Condition (1959-1961).

information.contentText: Tōkyō Monogatari is admired for its emotional depth. The film has appeared several times on the British Film Institute's lists of the 50 greatest films of all time, published by Sight & Sound magazine. In the critics' poll, it was ranked the 3rd (1992), 5th (2002) and 3rd (2012) greatest film of all time. In the directors' poll, it was ranked the 17th (1992), 16th (2002, tied with Psycho and The Mirror) and 1st (2012) greatest film of all time. In the latest poll, it received votes from 48 of the 358 directors surveyed. It also appears on Bravo magazine's list in 19th place.

content_list.content_text: In a more action-packed vein, filmmakers such as Hiroshi Inagaki (1905-1980) made stylized samurai films that, at their best, combine carefully choreographed violence with criticism of the feudal values that kept Japan backward for many centuries.

This variety of content and depth went hand in hand with the films' popularity: at their peak, Japanese studios enjoyed steady commercial success and, by the end of the 1950s, were producing around 500 films a year. Only in the following decade, as Japanese audiences turned their attention to foreign films or began staying home to watch television, did the film industry enter a period of decline.

The success of postwar Japanese cinema was due in part to the country's political stability at the time. Films made in the same period in other Eastern countries suffered more from the impact of history.

information.contentText: Wuya yu maque achieved its unique status in the history of Chinese cinema because of the long campaign of political criticism decreed against it. On May 20, 1951, after the editorial Ought to Emphasize the Discussion on 'The Life of Wu Xun' was published in the People's Daily, the first large-scale excoriation of a film in the history of the People's Republic of China began.

content_list.content_text: China, as an old Confucian saying predicted, was living through interesting times. Soon after the war, directors such as Zheng Junli (1911-1969) made socially critical films and developed an innovative visual style. Junli directed Wuya yu maque (Crows and Sparrows, 1949) when Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government was about to fall and be taken over by the communists; the film was only released after the civil war.

Many of these directors were leftists, but ironically, several of them suffered after Comrade Mao came to power. The harsh criticism of Yu Sun's Wu Xun zhuan (1950) - which tells the story of the 19th-century cultural hero Wu Xun - ushered in a period of heavy state intervention in the Chinese film industry. Nationalization and strict rules on subject matter practically stamped out cinematic creativity in the 1950s.

quote.quote: Seven Samurai is long, it is brutal, it is always hard to follow. But it is magnificent.
quote.author: Dilys Powell on Seven Samurai (1954)

content_list.content_text: A hesitant liberalization at the end of the decade allowed some notable films to be made in the mid-1960s, perhaps the most famous of which was Xie Jin's (1923-2008) melodrama Wutai jiemei (Two Stage Sisters, 1964). The Cultural Revolution of 1966, however, led to a temporary halt of all film production in China.

The development of Korean cinema was also inhibited by politics. The Korean War ended with the peninsula divided into two separate countries, ruled by regimes of the far left and the far right, both with strict censorship. Despite this, in the 1950s South Korea produced some important films based on popular novels, such as Han Hyeong-mo's (1917-1999) Jayu buin (Madame Freedom, 1956), a story of adultery that became a major box office hit.

information.contentText: The film's most quoted line, mentioned in the contemporary Variety review and in later writing on South Korean cinema, is "Let's get out of here! Let's get out of here!".

content_list.content_text: At the end of that same decade, several important South Korean filmmakers emerged, among them Yu Hyun-mok (1925-2009), and in 1959 the country produced more than 100 films. Between the end of the Syngman Rhee regime in 1960 and the rise of Park Chung Hee's military dictatorship the following year, Yu managed to direct Obaltan (Aimless Bullet, 1961), a reflective and somber account of life in a poor village, considered by some critics the best Korean film of all time.

Farther west, the thriving Indian film industry began to win international admiration in the postwar period with the work of its greatest director, the Bengali Satyajit Ray (1921-1992), who drew attention with Pather Panchali (1955) and his next two films, which formed the Apu Trilogy. These films followed the life of a child from his rural origins through adolescence and adulthood, using personal experience as a microcosm of life in India.

Ray went on making incredible films in the following decades, such as Charulata (The Lonely Wife, 1964), a profound study of a married woman's loneliness. A more political engagement was visible in the work of another Bengali filmmaker, Ritwik Ghatak (1925-1976), whose naturalistic Nagarik (The Citizen, 1952) predated Pather Panchali but was not a commercial success. Later, he made his masterpiece, Meghe Dhaka Tara (The Cloud-Capped Star, 1960), about the tragic experience of a refugee woman in Calcutta.

information.contentText: Around the world, filmmakers such as Martin Scorsese, James Ivory, Abbas Kiarostami, Elia Kazan, Carlos Saura, Isao Takahata, Philip Kaufman, Wes Anderson and Danny Boyle have been influenced by the Apu Trilogy.

content_list.content_text: Ray's and Ghatak's contributions to Bengali-language films represent just one pole of Indian cinema. Another pole was represented by popular Hindi films, produced in the Bombay-based industry known as Bollywood, the maker of entertaining melodramatic films that mixed action, love stories and dance.

Subsequent emigration from the Indian subcontinent made Bollywood films known in the West, but in the 1950s few of these films were distributed internationally. Raj Kapoor's (1924-1988) Awaara (1951), however, was nominated for the Grand Prix at Cannes. Another filmmaker who directed notable films in a popular idiom was actor/director Guru Dutt (1925-1964), best known for Kaagaz ke Phool (Paper Flowers, 1959), a tragic account of a filmmaker's professional and marital decline.

In Sri Lanka, Lester James Peries (b. 1919), generally considered the country's finest filmmaker, debuted in 1956 with Rekava. Sinhalese cinema, like Bollywood, was dominated by stylized melodrama, but Peries's film brought a new realism to it with the story of the punishments inflicted on a boy who believes he has magical powers. Peries expresses a subtle critique of the country's traditional beliefs. There are also active film industries in the Philippines, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Pakistan, Iran and Central Asia.

information.contentTitle: Canção "Awaara Hoon" do filme O Vagabundo (1951)
information.contentText: The song "Awaara Hoon" and actor Raj Kapoor were widely known in China and the Soviet Union. The film's success in the Soviet Union and China was attributed to the socialist themes it expressed. Awaara and the song "Awaara Hoon" are believed to have been among Chairman Mao's favorite film and song, respectively.

content_list.content_text: Since World War II, the cinema of these countries has remained little known internationally, but there may be gems waiting to be discovered. After all, few people in the West in 1945 imagined that the then-unknown Asian cinema could have directors of the stature of Kenji Mizoguchi or Satyajit Ray.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Alexander Jacoby , published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp.

movies.title: Seven Samurai
movies.overview: A samurai answers a village's request for protection after he falls on hard times. The town needs protection from bandits, so the samurai gathers six others to help him teach the people how to defend themselves, and the villagers provide the soldiers with food. A giant battle occurs when 40 bandits attack the village.

movies.title: Tokyo Story
movies.overview: The elderly Shukishi and his wife, Tomi, take the long journey from their small seaside village to visit their adult children in Tokyo. Their elder son, Koichi, a doctor, and their daughter, Shige, a hairdresser, don't have much time to spend with their aged parents, and so it falls to Noriko, the widow of their younger son who was killed in the war, to keep her in-laws company.

movies.title: Pather Panchali
movies.overview: Impoverished priest Harihar Ray, dreaming of a better life for himself and his family, leaves his rural Bengal village in search of work. Alone, his wife, Sarbojaya, looks after her rebellious daughter, Durga, and her young son, Apu, as well as Harihar's elderly aunt Indir. The children enjoy the small pleasures of their difficult life, while their parents suffer the daily indignities heaped upon them.

movies.title: Aparajito
movies.overview: The Unvanquished is the second part of the Apu film trilogy about the boy, Apu who gets a scholarship to study at a College in Calcutta. His mother is alone and torn between wanting him to be successful and not wanting him to leave her alone.

movies.title: The World of Apu
movies.overview: Apu is a jobless ex-student dreaming vaguely of a future as a writer. An old college friend talks him into a visit up-country to a village wedding....

movies.title: Rashomon
movies.overview: Brimming with action while incisively examining the nature of truth, "Rashomon" is perhaps the finest film ever to investigate the philosophy of justice. Through an ingenious use of camera and flashbacks, Kurosawa reveals the complexities of human nature as four people recount different versions of the story of a man's murder and the rape of his wife.

movies.title: Yojimbo
movies.overview: A nameless ronin, or samurai with no master, enters a small village in feudal Japan where two rival businessmen are struggling for control of the local gambling trade. Taking the name Sanjuro Kuwabatake, the ronin convinces both silk merchant Tazaemon and sake merchant Tokuemon to hire him as a personal bodyguard, then artfully sets in motion a full-scale gang war between the two ambitious and unscrupulous men.

movies.title: The Human Condition I: No Greater Love
movies.original_title: 人間の條件　第１部純愛篇／第２部激怒篇
movies.overview: A Japanese pacifist, unable to face the dire consequences of conscientious objection, is transformed by his attempts to compromise with the demands of war-time Japan.

movies.title: The Human Condition II: Road to Eternity
movies.original_title: 人間の條件　第３部望郷篇／第４部戦雲篇
movies.overview: As a conscript in war-time Japan's military, a pacifist struggles to maintain his determination to keep his ideals.

movies.title: The Human Condition III: A Soldier's Prayer
movies.original_title: 人間の條件　完結篇
movies.overview: His ideals challenged by life as a conscript in war-time Japan's military, a pacifist faces ever greater tests in his fight for survival.

movies.title: Madame Freedom
movies.overview: A professor's wife, O Seon-yeong (Kim Jeung-rim), starts working at a boutique shop. She meets Choe Yun-ju (No Gyung-hui) and goes to a dance party. She happens to like Sin Chun-ho (Lee Min), so she learns dancing from the next-door neighbor. Meanwhile, professor Jang (Park Am) is attracted to his student (Yang Mi-hui), who works as a typist. But he does not want to ruin his family while waiting for his wife to come home. In the end O realizes her mistake and comes back home with regret.

movies.title: Crows and Sparrows
movies.overview: At a Shanghai apartment, Mr Hou, a Nationalist official, gets ready to move to Taiwan upon the imminent defeat of the KMT during the Civil War. Mrs Hou gives an ultimatum to the rest of the tenants to move out on behalf of her husband, who is the "owner" of the flat and who is now planning to sell it. From the conversations with the rest, we find out that Hou has been a Hanjian during the Sino-Japanese War and that he has since taken over the apartment by force from the old landlord, Mr Kong.  The tenants, including Mr Kong, Mrs Xiao, Little Broadcast (alias Mr Xiao, played by Zhao Dan) and a schoolteacher, Mr Hua, and his wife, initially plan to band together, but circumstances force them to find other ways out. Mr Hua tries to find a place to stay at the KMT-sponsored school he is teaching in. Little Broadcast and Mrs Xiao invest in black market gold. As the situation escalates, Mr Hua gets arrested by KMT agents and his young daughter falls desperately ill.

content_list.subtitle: The events that shaped the world
content_list.title: Timeline of Events from 1940 to 1959
content_list.description: Asian cinema gains even more prominence with the release of several masterpieces. Film noir emerges and musicals continue to shine on the big screen. The Western holds on to its reign as one of the most popular genres, and one of the most important movements in cinema takes place in France: the French New Wave.
